Spring exhibition

Notes on the pictures, in the order they hang

The first room is given over to landscape. The paintings are small, and are hung low so that you must lean in, as if peering through a window. Notice how little the artist needs to say about the sky.

Beside the large marsh painting hangs a study of a gate, no bigger than a postcard. It was made on the same morning, according to the label, and it has the same cold light in it. The small picture floats to the left of this text, and the paragraph wraps around it for as long as it needs to, and then continues beneath at full width once the picture has ended.

The second paragraph does the same job, though by now the picture is almost behind us. It is a useful test of whether the lines make way for the float and then return to the full measure at the right moment.

Inline pictures sit on the text line: middle, baseline, top, text-bottom, all in one flowing paragraph that wraps onto a second line.

“I paint what I see until I see something else.”

The framed portrait floats right, with a heavy border and padding that count toward its size. The quotation to its left is indented on both sides and shortens its lines accordingly. Both belong to the second room, which is darker and quieter than the first and where most visitors linger.
